content: Halofantrine, quinine, and quinidine, including Coartem Tablets, have been associated with prolongation of the QT interval on the electrocardiogram. Patients with long QT syndrome or other clinical conditions known to prolong the QTc interval, such as a history of symptomatic cardiac arrhythmias, clinically relevant bradycardia, or severe cardiac disease, should avoid these medications. Additionally, individuals with a family history of congenital QT interval prolongation or sudden death, as well as those with hypokalemia or hypomagnesemia, are at increased risk. The use of QT-prolonging drugs, including antimalarials such as quinine and quinidine, should be approached with caution following the administration of Coartem Tablets. This is due to the long elimination half-life of lumefantrine (3–6 days) and the potential for additive effects on the QT interval. If the use of QT-prolonging drugs is medically necessary, ECG monitoring is recommended. Halofantrine and Coartem Tablets should not be administered within one month of each other because of the long elimination half-life of lumefantrine and the potential for additive QT interval effects. Antimalarials should not be given concomitantly with Coartem Tablets unless no other treatment options are available, as safety data in such scenarios are limited. If mefloquine is administered immediately prior to Coartem Tablets, there may be a decreased exposure to lumefantrine, possibly due to a mefloquine-induced reduction in bile production. Patients should be monitored for decreased efficacy, and food consumption should be encouraged while taking Coartem Tablets to enhance drug absorption. Coartem Tablets, when co-administered with substrates of CYP3A4, may result in decreased concentrations of the substrate and a potential loss of efficacy. Conversely, co-administration with CYP3A4 inhibitors, including grapefruit juice, may increase concentrations of artemether and/or lumefantrine, potentially exacerbating QT prolongation. Co-administration with CYP3A4 inducers may decrease concentrations of artemether and/or lumefantrine, reducing antimalarial efficacy. Drugs with mixed effects on CYP3A4, such as HIV protease inhibitors and non-nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors, as well as those affecting the QT interval, should be used cautiously in patients taking Coartem Tablets. Coartem Tablets may reduce the effectiveness of hormonal contraceptives. Patients using oral, transdermal patch, or other systemic hormonal contraceptives should be advised to use an additional non-hormonal method of birth control. Administration of Coartem Tablets with drugs metabolized by CYP2D6 may significantly increase plasma concentrations of the co-administered drug, raising the risk of adverse effects. Examples of such drugs include flecainide, imipramine, amitriptyline, and clomipramine. Food enhances the absorption of artemether and lumefantrine following the administration of Coartem Tablets. Patients who remain averse to food during treatment should be closely monitored, as the risk of recrudescence may be higher. In cases of recrudescent Plasmodium falciparum infection after treatment with Coartem Tablets, patients should be treated with a different antimalarial drug. The efficacy and safety of Coartem Tablets have not been studied in patients with severe hepatic and/or renal impairment. Limited data (43 patients) suggest that Coartem Tablets are effective in treating the erythrocytic stage of Plasmodium vivax infection. However, relapsing malaria caused by P. vivax requires additional treatment with an 8-aminoquinoline drug, such as primaquine, to eradicate hypnozoite forms that may remain dormant in the liver.
